steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The pawn offer is the sharpest sideline of the Italian Game. The price is a pawn, which is real material.

steps.text: **How to judge a gambit.** Emanuel Lasker (Common Sense in Chess, lectures of 1895) treats a gambit as a pawn traded for time and open lines, to be judged by whether the compensation survives the first accurate reply [V-sheet]. He gives a whole lecture to the Evans and judged its normal position good for White even a pawn down [V-sheet]. That is an 1890s judgement. A modern engine puts the main line near level, about +0.08 at depth 22 [V], so we test his view instead of trusting it.

**Morphy's view.** Paul Morphy reportedly thought the Evans was lost for White against careful defence; this comes second-hand [R, project sheet on Morphy]. Our engine check puts the main line near level, so the strong form of that claim does not survive. [V] One engine, one depth, not a verdict on the opening.

steps.text: **Plans in the Evans structure.** White: finish development, rebuild the d4 and e4 centre, and use the queen and bishop against f7 and the uncastled king. Black: give the pawn back at the right moment, usually with ...d5, or keep the bishop on a safe diagonal and trade pieces. Lasker (Lecture 4) listed three Black plans: advance the f-pawn, attack on the queenside, or break with a c-pawn move, and compared them by counting tempi [V-sheet]. [H] An engine finds resources he did not list.

steps.text: **Why the order matters.** If the b-pawn goes first, nothing defends it, so the capture is real and White must earn the pawn back. If c3 is already played, ...Bxb4 cxb4 Nxb4 gives Black two pawns for a bishop, a clear loss [V, depth 16]. [I] A rule of thumb to test: count who defends the pawn before pushing it. None: it is an offer and needs compensation. Defended by c3: it is a push, and taking it loses material.

steps.text: **The mark of a real gambit.** In the main line c3 gains a tempo on the bishop and d4 gains another by attacking e5; castling is simply development. With the pawn already on d3, ...Bxb4 comes with check and White gets no tempo. [H] A useful test for a pawn offer: count the tempi it gains. Two or more makes a gambit; none makes a loss. This is my rule of thumb, and I have not checked it against many gambits.

**What to remember.**
- A gambit pays a pawn for time, centre and lines.
- Judge it by whether the compensation survives the accurate reply. [V-sheet]
- Black accepts and hits back, or declines.
- Pawn c3 first makes a push; b4 first makes a gambit.
- With d3 played or a knight on f6, the offer fails. [V]
